lead: ZigBee and Z-Wave are two low-power wireless mesh protocols built for control, not for streaming. A light switch sends a few bytes; it must run for years on a coin cell and still reach a lamp three rooms away. Both solve this by forming a mesh: every mains-powered node forwards packets for its neighbours. ZigBee rides on IEEE 802.15.4 at 2.4 GHz and appears in smart homes, smart meters and street lighting. Z-Wave uses its own sub-GHz radio and dominates consumer home automation. This chapter covers both stacks and where each one wins.
prereq: You need Chapter 3.2 on IEEE 802.15.4 for the PHY and MAC layers that ZigBee reuses.

sections.h3: The ZigBee stack and device roles

blocks.text: ZigBee reuses IEEE 802.15.4 for its bottom two layers and adds the rest. The 802.15.4 PHY gives 16 channels at 2.4 GHz with 250 kbit/s, or regional 868/915 MHz channels at 20 and 40 kbit/s. The MAC gives CSMA/CA, a 64-bit IEEE address per device, and a 16-bit short address handed out by a parent at join time.

The NWK (network) layer builds the mesh. A coordinator starts the network: it picks a channel, a PAN ID (network identifier) and its own short address, usually 0x0000. Three topologies are allowed — star, tree and mesh. Tree routing is arithmetic: each parent owns a block of addresses, so a node can test whether the destination lies in its own subtree and pass the packet down, or send it up to its parent. Mesh routing is on-demand, a simplified AODV: a node with no route broadcasts a route request, the destination replies, and routers keep a route entry for a while. On-demand routing costs a burst of broadcasts but needs no periodic table exchange.

Device roles follow from this. One coordinator per network forms and manages it. Routers are mains-powered nodes that forward packets and accept children. End devices do not forward; a sleepy end device switches its radio off and its parent buffers frames until it polls. In 802.15.4 terms the coordinator and routers are full-function devices and the end device is a reduced-function device.

Above NWK sits the APS (Application Support Sublayer). APS gives a device up to 240 endpoints, numbered 1 to 240, which work like ports: endpoint 1 might be a light, endpoint 2 a temperature sensor. Inside an endpoint sit clusters, each a numbered group of attributes and commands. The On/Off cluster has ID 0x0006 and an attribute onOff. A profile ID ties a set of clusters into one application: Home Automation (0x0104), Smart Energy (0x0109) for metering and load control, Light Link (0xC05E) for touch-to-pair lamps, and Commercial Building Automation. Some syllabi call these application profiles, others the ZigBee application layer. Endpoint 0 is reserved for the ZDO (ZigBee Device Object), which handles joining, discovery and binding. A binding is a stored rule that sends frames from one endpoint and cluster to another, so a switch reaches a lamp without asking each time.

Security has two layers. The network key is shared by all nodes and protects each hop: a router decrypts a frame, checks it and re-encrypts it for the next hop, so every router can read network-protected payloads. The APS key is end-to-end between two devices and hides application data from routers. The trust center, normally the coordinator, decides who may join and hands out the network key. A device can be pre-loaded with a link key or an install code so the key exchange never travels in the clear.

Z-Wave is a competing mesh for home automation, defined by ITU-T G.9959. It does not use 802.15.4. It transmits in sub-GHz ISM bands, about 868 MHz in Europe and 908 MHz in North America, using GFSK at 9.6, 40 or 100 kbit/s. A lower frequency means a lower data rate but better penetration through walls and no competition from Wi-Fi. Each network has a 32-bit home ID and 8-bit node IDs, so one controller manages up to 232 nodes. A controller, primary or secondary, owns the routing table and the inclusion process; slaves only follow commands. Z-Wave uses source routing — the controller writes the whole route into the frame header — so slaves need almost no routing logic, which keeps them cheap. Z-Wave Plus added network-wide inclusion, explorer frames and the 100 kbit/s rate.

The trade-off is clear. ZigBee runs at 2.4 GHz, 250 kbit/s, 16 channels, sharing the band with Wi-Fi and microwave ovens; many vendors make chips; the standard is open but certified. Z-Wave runs sub-GHz at up to 100 kbit/s with one channel per region, meets less interference, comes from a single chip vendor (Silicon Labs) and requires certification, which keeps its ecosystem tighter. For a battery switch in a concrete house, Z-Wave's penetration wins. For a large smart-meter rollout that needs many vendors, ZigBee wins.

examples.question: A ZigBee home network has 1 coordinator, 4 routers and 20 end devices. Each router can accept 6 children and the coordinator can also accept 6. (a) Can all 20 end devices join directly to a parent? (b) If 2 routers fail, how many end devices lose their parent?
steps: Parent nodes that can accept children = coordinator + routers = 1 + 4 = 5.
20 end devices ≤ 30 slots, so yes, all can join; 30 − 20 = 10 slots stay free.
examples.answer: Yes, 30 slots cover 20 devices; after 2 routers fail only 18 slots remain, so 2 end devices lose their parent.
examples.check:
coordinator = 1
routers = 4
end_devices = 20
children_per_parent = 6
parents = coordinator + routers
slots = parents * children_per_parent
print(slots)
routers_after = routers - 2
parents_after = coordinator + routers_after
slots_after = parents_after * children_per_parent
print(slots_after)
print(end_devices - slots_after)

examples.question: A Z-Wave frame carries a 64-byte payload at 40 kbit/s. How long does the payload take to transmit, in milliseconds?
steps: At 100 kbit/s the same payload takes 512 ÷ 100,000 = 5.12 ms — 2.5 times faster.
examples.answer: The 64-byte payload takes 12.8 ms at 40 kbit/s and 5.12 ms at 100 kbit/s.

traps: Classic ZigBee is not IP-based. ZigBee IP is a separate profile; if you need IPv6 over 802.15.4, that is 6LoWPAN and RPL (Chapter 3.5).
Z-Wave is not built on 802.15.4 and is not at 2.4 GHz. It is ITU-T G.9959 in sub-GHz bands.
Network security is hop-by-hop and APS security is end-to-end: a router can read a network-protected frame but not an APS-protected one.
An end device never routes, and a sleepy end device's parent buffers its downlink frames. Exactly one coordinator exists per ZigBee network.
250 kbit/s belongs to the 2.4 GHz ZigBee PHY; 20 and 40 kbit/s belong to the 868/915 MHz PHYs. Do not mix them in a calculation.

quiz.q: Name the three ZigBee device roles and give one job of each.
quiz.a: Coordinator: forms the network, picks channel and PAN ID, acts as trust center. Router: forwards packets and accepts children. End device: hosts the application, does not forward, and may sleep.

quiz.q: Why does a ZigBee network have a trust center?
quiz.a: It controls joining and distributes the network key, so only approved devices get the shared key. Without it, any device in radio range could join and read traffic.

quiz.q: A Z-Wave frame carries 64 bytes at 40 kbit/s. Find the transmission time in ms, and again at 100 kbit/s.
ZigBee uses on-demand AODV-like routing instead of periodic table updates. Give one advantage and one cost.
quiz.a: Advantage: no periodic routing traffic, so sleepy nodes and low-duty-cycle networks save energy and bandwidth. Cost: the first packet to a new destination waits for a route request/reply broadcast, adding delay and a burst of traffic.

quiz.q: What is the difference between an endpoint and a cluster in APS?
quiz.a: An endpoint is a numbered address (1–240) inside one device, like a port. A cluster is a numbered set of attributes and commands (such as On/Off, 0x0006) inside an endpoint. Endpoint 0 is the ZDO.

quiz.q: Which standard defines Z-Wave's radio layer, and what modulation does it use?
quiz.a: ITU-T G.9959; GFSK modulation in sub-GHz ISM bands.

quiz.q: A factory hall runs both ZigBee at 2.4 GHz and Wi-Fi. Which is more likely to lose packets, and what would you change?
quiz.a: ZigBee is more exposed: Wi-Fi uses 20 MHz channels that overlap several of ZigBee's 2 MHz channels, and Wi-Fi has higher transmit power. Fix by moving ZigBee to channels away from the Wi-Fi channel (for example Wi-Fi on 1 and ZigBee near 25), lowering ZigBee transmit power, or using a sub-GHz technology such as Z-Wave or WirelessHART for critical loops.

beyond: Not for the exam. ZigBee 3.0 merged the older profiles into one base device behaviour, so a single chip can be commissioned into any ZigBee network. Thread, an IETF standard also on 802.15.4, competes with ZigBee by carrying IPv6 natively; Matter then runs over Thread and Wi-Fi. Z-Wave Long Range moves to a star topology with roughly 1 km range. Search for ZigBee 3.0 base device, Z-Wave S2 security and Matter device types.
